query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Strong nanoparticle–support interactions mediated by a high density of specific surface defects (e.g., vacancy clusters and wrinkled edge planes in turbostratic graphite) govern the preservation of HEA nanoparticle stability under high-temperature conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy nanoparticles deposited on carbon-based supports that have a high density of well-defined defects such as exposed edge planes and vacancy clusters.
generation.intervention: Engineer the support surface to have a controlled, high density (quantified via pre-characterization, e.g., via Raman and BET defect analysis) of atomic-scale defects versus supports that have been treated to passivate or reduce defect density.
generation.conditions: Catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric conditions up to ~1923 K, where both nanoparticle–support binding and support integrity are critical.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanoparticle–support interface featuring abundant vacancy sites and wrinkled edge planes, which create high binding energies that lower atomic mobility on the support.
generation.mechanism: Defect sites on the support, when present at high density, provide strong anchoring that not only minimizes nanoparticle mobility (preventing sintering) but also resists moderate support degradation. In contrast, supports with low defect density do not offer sufficient anchoring, leading to sintering under thermal stress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles on defect‐rich carbon supports will remain well dispersed and resist coarsening after prolonged exposure to high temperatures, whereas those on passivated or low defect density supports will exhibit significant agglomeration and phase coalescence.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles supported on standard, unmodified carbon surfaces with typical, moderate defect density.
generation.boundary: This mechanism holds when the support’s intrinsic thermal stability is maintained and defect density exceeds a critical threshold; if the support undergoes severe degradation or if defect density is below ~ a pre-determined level, the enhanced stabilization effect may be lost.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative benefit of defect-rich supports is established, the exact quantitative threshold for defect density and the degree of support degradation that can be tolerated remain to be further quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two catalyst samples: one with carbon supports engineered to have high defect density and another with supports treated to minimize defects. Subject both to identical high-temperature treatments and then characterize using in situ TEM, Raman spectroscopy, and BET analysis.
measurements: TEM imaging for particle size distribution and sintering evaluation
Raman spectroscopy to quantify defect density before and after treatment
XRD for phase identification and stability measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no statistically significant difference in nanoparticle dispersion or phase stability between the high-defect and low-defect support samples after thermal treatment, the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Further in situ annealing studies up to 1173 K also confirms the excellent thermal stability of nanoparticles. We believe the mechanistic details reported in this work would not only guide the nanoparticles synthesis through Joule heating-based methods, but also pave the way on understanding other rapid high temperature synthesis approaches.

cited_evidence.text: The MD simulations indicates that the nanoparticles are quite stable on the edge planes of T-graphite even at extremely high temperatures. To further verify the thermal stability of such nanoparticles, we performed in situ TEM heating on the CNFs decorated with Pt nanoparticles that were synthesized through ex situ Joule heating method. The ex situ formed nanoparticles appear to have very similar morphology to the in situ observations reported in this work. As it can be seen in Fig. 7a, the ultra-fine nanoparticles are located at wrinkled edge planes showing FCC structure (inset of Fig. 7a). The Pt-decorated CNFs are evaluated at various temperatures (573 K, 773 K, 973 K, and 1173 K). As shown in the high angle annular dark field (HAADF)-STEM image in Fig. 7b, the ultra-small Pt nanoparticles are well dispersed on CNF at room temperature (RT).
